identityReview: Kevin Michael Rudd, born Nambour, Queensland, 21 September 1957; Australian diplomat and former parliamentarian, twice prime minister, foreign minister between premierships, US ambassador March 2023–March 2026, now Asia Society Global President and CEO. Preserve earned ANU honours BA and Oxford research DPhil. Correct stale current-ambassador labels, distinguish whole Society from its Policy Institute, and keep party ballots, parliamentary elections and prime-ministerial oaths/cessation separate.
lifeStatusEvidence: University of Zurich Global Affairs records Rudd’s actual State of Asia Address and Q&A on 4 November 2026, identifying him as Asia Society Global President and CEO. UZH News’s 6 November retrospective corroborates the completed appearance. His personal transcript is dated 5 November, a separate publication label, and is not used to move the event date.

sourceReview.accessMethod: Read selected National Archives biography, timeline and office-history sections; ANU alumni and 2026 lecture paragraphs; National Museum apology account; one-page UN treaty notification; 2013 prime-ministerial asylum announcement and UNHCR briefing; 2022 and 2026 diplomatic announcements; the Asia Society announcement reproduced on Rudd’s site and current personal biography; two Zurich retrospective accounts; ABC credentials-page text; Commons image history and DFAT copyright statement. Individual scope and conflicts are recorded.
corrections: Read the National Archives fast-facts profile: Nambour, Queensland, 21 September 1957; ANU BA (Honours) 1981; prime minister 3 December 2007–24 June 2010 and 27 June–18 September 2013; foreign minister in 2010–2012. Party leadership dates differ from prime-ministerial office dates. Its parliamentary-service line starts 10 November 1998, whereas its separate timeline gives election on 3 October; the public chronology explicitly uses election date rather than treating the two entries as identical. Older open-ended after-office entries are not proof of current roles.

Read the ANU alumni page’s degree and career paragraphs. The heading specifies BA (Asian Studies) (Hons), 1981. It records diplomatic service 1981–1988, Stockholm and Beijing postings, then chief of staff to Wayne Goss as opposition leader and later premier from 1989, followed by state cabinet-office leadership 1992–1995 and consulting. Goss was not already premier throughout the chief-of-staff period. Its statement of two re-elections is historically incomplete, not a basis to erase later parliamentary terms. No honorary-degree substitution for the earned bachelor’s degree.

Read selected sections on inauguration, climate, apology, financial-crisis response, implementation criticism and the second term. They establish stimulus and bank-deposit guarantees, criticism of school-building and insulation execution, 26 June 2013 party vote, 7 September election defeat, 18 September successor-government formation and 22 November resignation from Parliament. Exact spending totals, claims of sole economic causation and the page’s compressed G20 founding narrative are not adopted. Its climate wording calls December 2007 a signing; the UN depositary distinguishes ratification and entry into force. The surrounding international-travel chronology contains questionable year labels and is not used. No full audit, royal-commission report or economic causal study was reviewed.

Read the National Archives timeline entries for 3 October 1998 Griffith election and 4 December 2006 Labor parliamentary leadership. This page labels the apology 14 February 2008, conflicting with the museum, parliamentary sources and even the Archives’ during-office photo captions; public text uses 13 February. The description of Gillard as Australia’s first deputy prime minister omits the important woman qualifier and is not reproduced. The Kyoto item is not treated as proof of a new treaty signature on 3 December.

Read the National Museum’s opening account and relevant apology context. It establishes the formal national apology on 13 February 2008 to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, especially the Stolen Generations affected by forced child removal and assimilation. The 1995 inquiry and subsequent reconciliation process predate the apology. Do not claim the apology itself eliminated disadvantage or that Rudd personally originated every reconciliation effort. No long speech quotation or full inquiry review is claimed.

Read the one-page UN depositary notification C.N.1243.2007.TREATIES-12. Australia’s ratification was effected on 12 December 2007; Article 25(3) set entry into force for Australia on 11 March 2008. This is distinct from domestic signing of the ratification instrument and the 3 December inauguration. The declaration about emissions accounting is not expanded into unreviewed legal interpretations. Text extraction was read, not a screenshot or a full national implementation audit.

Read the relevant 19 July 2013 prime-ministerial media-release paragraphs: unauthorized boat arrivals without visas were to be sent to PNG for assessment, with recognized refugees settled there. Deterrence and lifesaving language is the government’s rationale, not proof of outcomes. The transcript-site header lists a service end of 7 September 2013, the election date; it is not adopted over official prime-ministerial term records ending 18 September. The exact signed bilateral instrument and all subsequent amendments were not read.

Read UNHCR’s 26 July 2013 briefing note in full through its substantive protection assessment. It acknowledges dangerous voyages and Australia’s resettlement contribution, but identifies inadequate safeguards, processing capacity, arbitrary/open-ended detention, integration challenges and Australia’s continuing shared responsibility with PNG. These are attributed institutional findings, not a criminal conviction of Rudd. This accessible briefing is distinct from the separate story page that returned 429 and whose indexed dateline anomalously says August despite a July heading.

Read the joint prime-minister/foreign-minister release dated 13 January 2026, including the closing sentence setting the posting end at 31 March and the retrospective March 2023 start. January is an announcement, not immediate departure; later university reports and the current biography confirm the role ended. Its list includes prospective March 2026 summit language among achievements, so the whole list is not blindly treated as completed on 13 January. AUKUS, investment and diplomatic-outcome claims are not independently audited or assigned solely to Rudd.

Read the opening Asia Society board announcement reproduced on Rudd’s site, dated 12 January 2026 in New York. It sets a 31 March return as president and CEO, separates Society-wide service in 2021–2023 from founding Policy Institute leadership in 2015–2023, and identifies the China-analysis centre established in 2022. It is an institutional announcement carried on his site, not an independent report of attendance on the handover day. The public entry uses March and subsequent confirmation rather than inventing a witnessed handover ceremony.

Read the current personal biography’s role, return and education paragraphs. It states Global President and CEO, March 2026 return after the US posting, and Oxford DPhil awarded in 2022 on Xi Jinping’s ideological worldview. ANU and Zurich provide independent institutional corroboration of education and current activity. Self-promotional rankings, sole-founder language about the G20, and claims of the world’s best stimulus strategy are not adopted as independently established facts.

Read the University of Zurich Global Affairs retrospective dated 4 November 2026, including actual speech, Q&A, and current Asia Society title. It expressly dates the event to 4 November and describes his views on US–China relations and Europe. The captions identify conversation with Remko Tanis; no photo pixels or full video were inspected. Forecasts about Chinese leadership tenure or geopolitical stability are attributed analysis, not factual guarantees. The university’s separate research partnerships do not establish that Rudd founded or leads those projects.

Read the opening of UZH News’s 6 November 2026 retrospective. It confirms that Rudd actually spoke in the university auditorium, was formerly ambassador earlier that year, had two premierships with foreign-minister service between, and completed doctoral research in 2022. The article’s publication date is not the speech date. The full video, all speech claims and every underlying international-policy development were not reviewed.

Read the ABC video-page title, 20 April 2023 publication timestamp and repeated explanatory sentence stating that he had presented credentials to President Biden. The embedded 2-minute-41-second video was not watched. This establishes a completed credentials presentation by publication, not an exact presentation date, and is distinct from the March posting start. The 2 May update is not a new appointment.

Read the relevant paragraphs of the 20 December 2022 joint diplomatic-appointment release. They announce the intention to appoint Rudd and an intended early-2023 posting. Do not confuse announcement with physical arrival, credentials presentation, or another appointee’s consul-general role. The later 2026 release confirms the actual posting began in March 2023; no exact March day is asserted.

Read the 4 September 2026 ANU account of his completed China in the World lecture and the education/career paragraphs. It identifies him as former US ambassador and Asia Society global president, confirms honours study in Chinese and East Asian history and subsequent Oxford DPhil on Xi’s worldview. Publication date is not assumed to be the exact lecture date. Rudd’s interpretation of ideology is attributed research, not an independently established prediction; the linked full video was not watched.

Read 5 November 2026 date and opening speech paragraphs. Zurich’s retrospective and indexed organizer podcast metadata identify actual delivery on 4 November. The joke about his next job in a Beijing embassy is not a new appointment.
Indexed organizer metadata says recorded 4 November 2026. Audio not listened to and full page not opened; the university account provides direct event evidence.
Search-indexed biography still calls him current ambassador despite the confirmed 2026 transition. Not adopted as current-office evidence; full page not read.

sourceReview.limits: AI editorial and translation review, not certified native-language or human review. No original degree certificates, full doctoral thesis, complete stimulus audit or royal-commission report, all asylum instruments and subsequent judgments, full event video/audio or portrait pixels were reviewed. Acknowledgment of policy significance does not establish that inequalities disappeared; institutional criticism is attributed and not a personal criminal judgment. Refresh current office before publication.

portraitReview.unresolved: Read Commons description, DFAT attribution/license template and file history, then the actual DFAT copyright statement. It licenses site material under CC BY 4.0 except the Commonwealth Coat of Arms and otherwise noted material. The portrait is described as 2023; initial 26 March 2023 03:49 upload by DraftSaturn15 was 768×1151, 73 KB from the embassy staff-profile URL. DTH89 replaced it on 5 April 2023 at 05:39 with a 3710×5562, 7.08 MB version from the DFAT head-of-mission page. Uploaders are not asserted to be photographers; source year is not an exact capture date. Existing cropped derivatives are not silently substituted. Prior cache data/research/cache/portraits/44b9797bd81e3c685d1ba94e.jpg (247995 bytes in evidence) is absent and does not establish possession of the 7.08 MB original. One original download on 18 November returned curl exit 22, 403 and HTTP 000. Identity, original colour, framing and sharpness remain unreviewed; preserve credit, license link and any later modifications.

translationReview.scope: All 32 display fields reviewed in seven foreign languages against Chinese and English. Preserve former/current ambassadorship and Society-wide versus Policy Institute roles; two nonconsecutive premierships with intervening foreign-minister service; 2013 party vote, oath, general election and formal departure; 1998 election versus parliamentary-service metadata; 13 February apology and correct Indigenous groups; Kyoto ratification versus entry into force; research DPhil versus honorary degree; asylum-announcement terms and attributed UNHCR concerns; March 2026 transition announcement versus later confirmation; 4 November Zurich event versus 5 and 6 November publications. Preserve institutional abbreviations and avoid claiming human native review.
